The Melbourne housing dataset contains 34,857 records and 21 variables describing property characteristics, locations, sale methods, and prices. Among records with observed prices, the median price is A$870,000 and the mean is approximately A$1.05 million. The higher mean and maximum price of A$11.2 million suggest a right-skewed distribution. Prices are missing for 7,610 records (21.8%), so price analyses will use only records with observed prices. Building area and year built also have substantial missingness, and some values warrant further investigation, including construction years ranging from 1196 to 2106 and unusually large land and building areas. The analysis will explore how prices vary across property types and regions and how they relate to distance from the city center, building area, and room count.
Questions to explore:
1. How do prices differ across property types and regions?
2. How does the mix of property types vary across regions?
3. How is price associated with distance from the city center?
4. How are building area and room count associated with price?

#Prepare variables for analysis
housing <- housing_raw |>
  mutate(
    property_type = factor(
      Type,
      levels = c("h", "t", "u"),
      labels = c("House", "Townhouse", "Unit/apartment")
    ),
    region = factor(
      na_if(na_if(str_trim(Regionname), ""), "#N/A")
    ),
    Price = if_else(Price > 0, Price, NA_real_),
    BuildingArea = if_else(BuildingArea > 0, BuildingArea, NA_real_)
  )

priced <- housing |>
  filter(!is.na(Price))



Contingency tables
The following one-way contingency tables summarize the number and percentage of records by property type and region. These describe the composition of the dataset, including records without observed prices.

#One-way contingency tables
type_counts <- housing |>
  count(property_type, name = "n", .drop = FALSE) |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * n / sum(n))

type_counts |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Property type", "Records", "Percent"),
    digits = 1,
    caption = "Distribution of records by property type."
  )

Houses account for most records (68.8%), followed by units/apartments (20.9%) and townhouses (10.3%). Southern Metropolitan has the largest share of records (34.0%), followed by Northern Metropolitan (27.4%) and Western Metropolitan (19.5%). The three Victoria regions have relatively few records, so comparisons involving these regions should consider their smaller sample sizes.
The two-way contingency table shows how property types are distributed across regions. Row percentages allow comparisons between regions with different numbers of records.

  filter(!is.na(region), !is.na(property_type))

  type_region_complete,
  table(region, property_type)
)

knitr::kable(
  addmargins(type_region_table),
  caption = "Property type by region: counts, excluding missing categories.",

Houses were the most common property type in every region. Their share ranged from 58.9% of records in Southern Metropolitan to more than 94% in each of the three Victoria regions. Southern Metropolitan had the highest proportion of units and apartments (29.9%), followed by Northern Metropolitan (21.3%). Comparisons involving the Victoria regions should be interpreted cautiously because those regions have fewer records.


Numerical summaries
The following table summarizes price, number of rooms, distance from the city center, and building area by property type. The number of observed values is reported for each variable because missingness differs across variables.

quantitative_by_type <- housing |>
  filter(!is.na(property_type)) |>
  select(property_type, Price, Rooms, Distance, BuildingArea) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -property_type,
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  group_by(property_type, variable) |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(value)),
    mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

quantitative_by_type |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    col.names = c(
      "Property type", "Variable", "Observed n",
      "Mean", "Median", "SD"
    ),
    caption = "Numerical summaries by property type."
  )

Houses had the highest median price at A$1,015,000, followed by townhouses at A$850,000 and units/apartments at A$580,000. For each property type, the mean was higher than the median, which suggests that some expensive properties may be raising the average.
Houses also had the largest median building area at 151 m², compared with 133 m² for townhouses and 75 m² for units/apartments. Houses were generally farther from the city centre, with a median distance of 11.2 km, while units/apartments had a median distance of 7.2 km. Both houses and townhouses had a median of three rooms, compared with two rooms for units/apartments.
Building area was missing for many properties, so these results are based on fewer observations. The standard deviation for house building area was especially large (454.1 m²), suggesting that there may be some unusually large values worth looking at more closely.


Plots

library(scales)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

type_colors <- c(
  "House" = "#0072B2",
  "Townhouse" = "#D55E00",
  "Unit/apartment" = "#009E73"
)

price_labels <- label_dollar(
  prefix = "A$",
  scale = 1e-6,
  suffix = "M"
)


1. Bar chart: property type

housing |>
  filter(!is.na(property_type)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = property_type)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#0072B2", width = 0.65) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Property Records by Type",
    x = "Property type",
    y = "Number of records"
  )




The bar chart shows that houses make up most of the records in the dataset, with 23,980 records (68.8%). Units and apartments are the second-largest group, with 7,297 records (20.9%), followed by townhouses, with 3,580 records (10.3%). This means that the dataset contains many more houses than the other two property types.


2. Side-by-side bar chart: property type and region

type_region_complete |>
  ggplot(aes(x = region, fill = property_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = type_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Property Types Across Regions",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Number of records",
    fill = "Property type"
  )




The chart shows that houses are the most common property type in every region. Southern Metropolitan has the most records for all three property types, followed by Northern Metropolitan. The three Victoria regions have much fewer records than the metropolitan regions. Because this chart shows counts, some of the differences reflect the number of records available in each region. The row percentages in the contingency table are more useful for comparing the mix of property types across regions.


3. Histogram: price

#logarithmic axis makes the spread of the right-skewed prices easier to see
priced |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#0072B2", color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = price_labels) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Observed Property Prices",
    subtitle = "Price is shown on a logarithmic scale",
    x = "Price (AUD; log scale)",
    y = "Number of records"
  )




The histogram shows that observed property prices are concentrated around A$1 million, with fewer properties at the low and high ends. On the logarithmic scale, the distribution appears roughly mound-shaped. I used a log scale because prices range widely, and a small number of expensive properties extend the upper end of the distribution. The log scale compresses those high values and makes the spread of the more common prices easier to see. The axis labels still show prices in Australian dollars, but equal distances on the axis represent equal multiplicative changes rather than equal dollar amounts.


4. Box plot: price by property type

priced |>
  filter(!is.na(property_type)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = property_type, y = Price, fill = property_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = type_colors) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = price_labels) +
  labs(
    title = "Property Prices by Type",
    subtitle = "Price is shown on a logarithmic scale",
    x = "Property type",
    y = "Price (AUD; log scale)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")




The box plot shows that houses had the highest median observed price, followed by townhouses and units/apartments. There is some overlap between the price ranges of the three property types, and each group has values outside the whiskers. Houses have the highest observed prices, including some above A$10 million.
The logarithmic scale makes it easier to compare the groups while still displaying the wide range of prices. The points outside the whiskers are potential outliers; they are not necessarily errors.


5. Scatter plot: price, distance, and property type

priced |>
  filter(!is.na(Distance), !is.na(property_type)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Distance, y = Price, color = property_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = type_colors) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = price_labels) +
  labs(
    title = "Property Price and Distance from Central Melbourne",
    subtitle = "Price is shown on a logarithmic scale",
    x = "Distance from city centre (km)",
    y = "Price (AUD; log scale)",
    color = "Property type"
  )




The scatter plot suggests that property prices generally decrease as distance from central Melbourne increases, although there is considerable variation at most distances. The highest-priced properties are mostly closer to the city center. Houses tend to have higher prices than units and apartments at similar distances, while the price ranges of the property types overlap.
Most records are within about 20 km of the city center, so there are fewer observations to compare at greater distances. The plot shows an association between price and distance, but other factors may also help explain the differences in price.


6. Faceted scatter plot: building area, price, rooms, and type

priced |>
  filter(
    !is.na(BuildingArea),
    !is.na(property_type),
    !is.na(Rooms)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = BuildingArea, y = Price, color = Rooms)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ property_type) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = price_labels) +
  labs(
    title = "Building Area and Price by Property Type",
    subtitle = "Both axes use logarithmic scales",
    x = "Building area (square metres; log scale)",
    y = "Price (AUD; log scale)",
    color = "Rooms"
  )




The faceted scatter plot suggests that larger properties generally have higher prices within each property type, although prices vary considerably for properties of similar sizes. Houses tend to have larger building areas and higher prices than units and apartments. The colors also suggest that properties with more rooms generally have larger building areas.
Both axes use logarithmic scales because building area and price have wide ranges. A few building-area values appear unusually small or large and may need further inspection. Since building area is missing for many records, this plot includes only a subset of the dataset.


7. Heatmap: median price by region and property type

heatmap_data <- priced |>
  filter(!is.na(region), !is.na(property_type)) |>
  group_by(region, property_type) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_price = median(Price),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    tile_label = paste0(
      dollar(median_price, prefix = "A$", scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"),
      "\nn = ", comma(n)
    )
  )

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = property_type, y = region, fill = median_price)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = tile_label), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#F7FBFF",
    high = "#6BAED6",
    labels = price_labels
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Price by Region and Property Type",
    subtitle = "Tiles show median price and number of observed prices",
    x = "Property type",
    y = "Region",
    fill = "Median price"
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())




The heatmap shows that median prices vary by both region and property type. Southern Metropolitan had the highest median price for houses (A$1.66 million) and townhouses (A$1.19 million). Across the metropolitan regions, houses had higher median prices than townhouses and units/apartments.
Some comparisons in the Victoria regions are based on very few observed prices. For example, the median for townhouses in Northern Victoria is based on just one record, so it should be interpreted cautiously. The blank tile for townhouses in Western Victoria indicates that there were no observed prices for that combination.
